# Between Development and Oversight: China’s Approach to Addressing Artificial Intelligence Risks ## **Artificial Intelligence Through the Lens of National Security: The Minister of State Security's Article** According to Chen, artificial intelligence lowers the cost and skill barrier for executing cyberattacks, enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities and the automation of attacks, and even “AI versus AI” confrontations.
At the same time, he points to the increasing integration of AI in intelligence, decision-making, target identification, operational support, and cognitive influence.
While Framework 3.0 (see below) emphasizes the risk of autonomous systems exceeding their assigned tasks or escaping human control, Chen focuses on how people, states, and hostile actors use AI—and on the risks posed by technological lag.
## **Risk Management: The Artificial Intelligence Safety Governance Framework 3.0** Artificial intelligence is thus viewed simultaneously as a source of national power and a potential threat.

# Watch:Videos [Air Force Doctrine Note 25-1 Artificial Intelligence](https://www.war.gov/Multimedia/Videos?videoid=958216)
[![Officers from the 173rd Airborne Brigade’s Bayonet Innovation Team are advocating for cutting-edge military advancements to enhance battlefield capabilities. 1st Lt. Bennett Hellman, 1st Lt. Francesco La Torre, and 1st Lt. Vincent Gasparri recently spoke on the role of innovation in modern warfare, emphasizing its necessity for maintaining superiority. "You need to innovate to survive and to stay ahead and to stay at the cutting edge," said La Torre, who previously served as an executive officer in an airborne rifle company within the 173rd Airborne Brigade. Hellman, an 11A infantry officer and director of data for the Bayonet Innovation Team, highlighted the role of artificial intelligence in shaping the brigade’s future. "As a brigade, the first step towards artificial intelligence on the battlefield is aggregating our data," he said. "One of the best things artificial intelligence offers is the ability to do things that humans aren't good at. Pattern recognition across millions of rows and thousands of columns isn't something that a human can do." Gasparri stressed the importance of improved communication and data proliferation. "I think that communication and our ability to proliferate and gather data—whether from UAS systems, different sensors, or even personnel across the battlefield—using technologies like Starlink, Star Shield terminals, new types of radios, and computing power, is essential,” he said. The officers pointed to real-world examples of innovation within the brigade, such as integrating drones into resupply missions. "Being able to protect troops or resupply formations by using drones is incredible and could save lives on the modern battlefield," Gasparri said. “We recently had non-tactical UAS operators get certified to fly FPV drones that they built themselves." Gasparri also described a recent test of an octocopter UAS system capable of carrying up to 200 kilograms of payload. item.title: Here’s How UMKC is Embracing Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
# [UMKC Today](https://umkc.edu/news) ## Here’s How UMKC is Embracing Artificial Intelligence Across UMKC, faculty are using artificial intelligence to tackle challenges in healthcare, business, law, education and beyond
As artificial intelligence becomes more prominent in our everyday lives, many faculty have been on the leading edge of using this technology in the classroom and in their respective fields.
"Artificial intelligence isn’t confined to a single discipline at UMKC,” said Sumeet Dua, vice chancellor for research and innovation. “While we are advancing core algorithms and autonomous systems, our researchers are also pairing computational methods with deep expertise across medicine, pharmacy, business, law and the humanities.
###### **Henry W. Bloch School of Management** Professor Nathan Mauck, Ph.D. is helping business professionals rethink and improve how they use artificial intelligence.
Through interactive exercises, participants practiced using AI as a thought partner.
The school also launched a [Master of Business Administration in Business Analytics](https://bloch.umkc.edu/graduate/degree-programs/mba-business-analytics.html) program to teach students how to leverage artificial intelligence, including large language models and emerging technology, to analyze complex data sets and inform strategy.
###### **School of Dentistry** Rose Wang, Ph.D., is combining artificial intelligence with infrared technology to identify precancerous oral lesions that are at high risk of developing into cancer.
Wang uses machine learning to analyze biochemical data from tissue samples collected through infrared spectroscopic imaging. The technology produces thousands of variables at each pixel, making manual analysis nearly impossible. Machine learning models help extract the most important information and provide an objective way to assess risk.
###### **School of Medicine** Saman Zeeshan, Ph.D., research assistant professor of biomedical and health informatics, is using artificial intelligence to find early warning signs of cancer.
Zeeshan’s lab, [UMKC LIONS](https://sites.google.com/view/zeeshan-lab/about) (Lab for Investigating Oncology Networks and Systems), performs cancer genomic and transcriptomic data analysis and AI/ML algorithm development. They have conducted multiple studies examining the application of AI in precision medicine and have built an AI framework that integrating multi-omics and phenotypic data through machine learning into a unified framework for disease prediction and patient profiling.
###### **School of Nursing and Health Studies** Many hospitals use AI documentation tools such as Suki, which listens as nurses work and drafts clinical notes automatically for them.
###### **School of Science and Engineering** Associate professor Mostafizur Rahman, Ph.D. leads a $3 million National Science Foundation Research Traineeship program that trains graduate students to use artificial intelligence to mitigate alcohol and drug abuse.
Master’s and doctoral students in the [AI-MADA](https://info.umkc.edu/ai-mada/) (Mitigating Alcohol and Drug Abuse Using Artificial Intelligence and Secure Networked Sensing) program learn to securely collect, store and analyze data on alcohol and drug abuse through the utilization of noninvasive sensing technologies, widespread wireless technologies and cloud-based cyber infrastructure. They also help build an AI reasoning engine that turns that data into insights about addiction.
The school also launched a [Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence](https://www.umkc.edu/news/posts/2026/february/umkc-announces-new-master-of-science-in-artificial-intelligence.html) program to lead AI-driven innovation in healthcare, cybersecurity and intelligent systems.

item.title: A Third of Young Adults Turn to Artificial Intelligence for Substance-Use Information
item.description:
# A Third of Young Adults Turn to Artificial Intelligence for Substance-Use Information ![Artificial Intelligence](https://www.rutgers.edu/sites/default/files/styles/16x9_full_default_1x/public/mireia_ai_hero.png?h=8b7966f8&itok=AhIDeoKH)
### Rutgers researchers examine trends in people using chatbots for medical advice Rutgers Health researchers used survey data from nearly 1,000 participants to examine the frequency and characteristics of people turning to generative artificial intelligence (AI), a subfield of AI that creates synthetic content in response to user prompts, for substance-related information and their perceptions around the results produced by AI.
Mauro, an associate professor at the Center for Pharmacoepidemiology and Treatment Science and [Rutgers School of Public Health](https://sph.rutgers.edu/), also found that Black and male participants were more likely to use AI for substance use–related purposes.
As AI continues to shape the substance-use information available to young adults, Triguero Roura and Mauro suggest additional research should explore how young adults interpret and understand the outputs of AI when it relates to drugs and alcohol as well as the implications of this new source of information on public health.
